paragraphs: We have already said that neither of these two composed a book on the commandments, but dissented from the majority in small matters, such as: [keeping] the Festival of Weeks on the first day [of the week], the prohibition of the fat-tail (alyah) and the rump-fat (ʿaqavah), [the prohibition of] the brother's daughter and the sister's daughter, and the like.

As for "al-Tiflīsī" — he held [the calendar] by the parting [of the moon from the sun], following the statement of "Ismaʿīl"; except that he dissented from him in that he took the head of the month from the day on which the parting falls. He has answers to questions of [certain] people which he ascribes to "Ḥīwī," and he also has pages on the permitting of meat.

As for "Mālik al-Ramlī" — it is reported of him that he stood at the Temple and reported that the rooster used to be offered upon the altar that was in this House — meaning "the altar of the LORD." This is the act of an ignorant man.
: Arabic al-alyah and al-ʿaqavah — the fat-tail (the fatty part of the sheep's tail) and the fat around the rump; the Karaites forbade them, as did al-Tiflīsī and al-Ramlī.
: That is: Ismaʿīl al-ʿUkbarī takes the head of the month from the moment of parting (the conjunction), whereas al-Tiflīsī takes it from the day after the parting.
: "Ḥīwī" — Ḥīwī al-Balkhī, the early biblical critic (late 9th c.); al-Tiflīsī wrote answers to his objections. Cf. Rosenthal, "Ḥīwī al-Balkhī," JQR 38–39 (1948).
: Q calls the tradition of al-Ramlī (a rooster on the altar) foolish — the rooster not being among the offerings of Leviticus.
